facts.title: feat(ci): release self-contained binaries from a preview tag
facts.description:
Part of #181 (the release itself, `0.1.0-preview.1`, follows after merge)

- **Self-contained single-file, not trimmed (OD24, OD32):** a trimmed publish warns in `Anthropic` and `YamlDotNet` (IL2104), and the decision was to trim only a warning-free publish. `-warnaserror` holds the untrimmed publish to zero warnings.
- **Compressed:** `EnableCompressionInSingleFile` halves the binary (88 to 44 MB on linux-x64) for about 60 ms more at startup (41 to 100 ms measured), next to a run that waits seconds on a model.
- **Locked publish (item moved from #163):** the six RIDs are declared in `Directory.Build.props`, so every project in the publish graph has them in its lock file. `PublishSingleFile` sits in the csproj, not on the command line: the single-file analyzer brings in `Microsoft.NET.ILLink.Tasks`, and a publish-only property left it out of the lock file (NU1004 in locked mode, reproduced). Its version comes from the SDK, so `global.json` now pins `10.0.111` with `rollForward: disable`; a different SDK fails with a clear "SDK not found" instead of a lock-file mismatch. Contributors need exactly that SDK now; `CONTRIBUTING.md` says so and why.
- **One version:** `Version` in the csproj is `0.1.0-preview.1` and the only place it is written. `ToolVersion` reads it for the User-Agent (was a hardcoded `0.1.0`) and for `toolVersion` in `changelog.json` (unchanged form, `+<sha>` included). The release workflow refuses a tag that does not match it.
- **`PackAsTool` removed:** the NuGet path (#37) is after the launch, and a tool package and a self-contained single-file publish pull in different directions. It comes back with #37.
- **Release workflow on `v*-preview*`:** checks the tag against the csproj and that it is on `main`, runs `ci.yml` on the tagged commit (now `workflow_call`), then builds and smoke-tests each binary on a runner of its own platform (`macos-15-intel` for osx-x64, `windows-11-arm` for win-arm64), then writes `SHA256SUMS`, attests every binary and creates a **draft** pre-release. Draft because `GitHubReleaseNotesWriter` fills an existing draft for the tag, so `chartula generate` writes its own notes before a person publishes.
- **Smoke test:** `--help` prints the usage, and `preview` without `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, outside any checkout, exits 1 with the hint naming the variable. That path loads configuration, DI and the provider package, so a single-file bundling fault crashes there.
- **PRs that change the build inputs** (`release.yml`, `global.json`, `Directory.Build.props`, the CLI csproj, lock files) run the binary jobs without releasing, so a broken platform shows before a tag. This PR is the first such run.
- `docs/versioning.md` describes release assets and the release steps instead of a NuGet package.

**Verified locally:** locked-mode publish for `linux-x64` and `win-arm64` (cross) with `-warnaserror`, zero warnings; the linux binary with an empty environment prints the usage (exit 0) and ends a `preview` with `Configuration error: No Anthropic API key found in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ...` (exit 1). The other five platforms are verified by this PR's `binary (...)` checks.

**Left for after merge:** tag ruleset for `v*`, then tag `v0.1.0-preview.1` on the merge commit.

Tests: `ToolVersionTests` (GitHub requests carry `Chartula/<csproj version>`, without build metadata); `ProvenanceWiringTests` unchanged; suite 637 green.

facts.title: fix(curation): pair a revert with what it takes back
facts.description:
Closes #206

- **Not internal any more:** `revert` maps to `Other` in `ConventionalCommitCategorizer`, so a revert is never filtered away and never leaves the changes it took back in the facts as shipped. `Other` rather than a new category: a new value would change the documented `category` values of `changelog.json`.
- **Pairing (`Curation/RevertPairing`):** before changes are resolved, a revert - `revert:`, `revert(scope):` or GitHub's `Revert "..."` - is paired with what it names in a form read without judgment:
  - a commit hash of at least 7 characters, with at least one digit so a word like "defaced" is not one, that is the prefix of exactly one commit in the range;
  - GitHub's revert button, `Reverts owner/repo#N` / `Reverts #N`.

  A pull request number in prose does not pair; it is as often context. Hashes are read from the description with hidden comments removed (#141).
- **What drops out:** the pull requests a revert names. The revert itself drops out too when everything it names was in the release - nothing shipped. When it names anything unresolvable here (an earlier release, an ambiguous prefix), it takes back what it matched and stays, so a removal a reader may have met stays visible. A revert reverted in the same release is undone, one level deep.
- **Data:** `PullRequestInfo` gains `CommitShas`, the range's commits that belong to each pull request. `GitHubPullRequestReader` already walked commit by commit; it now keeps that mapping instead of discarding it.
- The decision is recorded on #206; `docs/cli.md` describes what pairs and the limitation that remains (a change replaced without being reverted).

**Reproduced and verified on the real repository:** the fact base for `goldbarth/port-tidewatch` `v1.3.0`, built with the production git reader, GitHub reader, resolver, filter and fact-base builder (no model, no tokens), went from 10 facts including #59, #60 and #61 - three features #62 reverted in the same release - to 7: #69, #68, #67, #66, #65, #58, #57. The alpha run's `release-v1.3.0.md` had announced all three as new.

Tests: `RevertPairingTests` (the port-tidewatch shape drops the revert and its three targets and keeps the rest; a revert of an earlier release stays; a partly resolvable revert takes back what it matched and stays; GitHub's revert button pairs by number; a number in prose does not; reverting a revert keeps the original; an ambiguous hash pairs nothing; a feature naming a hash pairs nothing); `GitHubPullRequestReaderTests` (every commit of a pull request is recorded).

facts.title: feat(prompting): ask for identifiers from the facts as code spans
facts.description:
Closes #143

- The technical prompt now asks for each name a technical reader looks up - command, option, configuration key, file, type, method - as a code span, spelled exactly as the facts spell it, and for nothing in backticks the facts do not contain. Which words are identifiers cannot be decided in code without guessing, so it is asked for rather than inferred (#137 fixed the rendering-breaking part deterministically).
- "Spelled exactly as the facts spell it" is there for the rule-based check: it flags a backticked name it cannot find, case-insensitively, in the titles and descriptions, so a shortened or normalized name would become a flag.
- `EscapeAngleBrackets` already leaves code spans alone, so `release-<tag>.md` inside backticks renders as written.
- Customer and product prompts are unchanged (out of scope).
- The prompt snapshot (#180) did its job: `technical.txt` and `prompt-hash.txt` failed until updated, and the diff above is the prompt change.

**Draft until the run the issue asks for.** One run on this repository, technical only, then read the identifiers and the rule-based flags, and accept the result rather than iterate (circuit breaker):

```bash
chartula preview --tag v0.1.0-preview.1 --whole-history --audience technical
```

Tests: `PromptSnapshotTests` with the updated snapshots; the suite otherwise unchanged (627).

facts.title: fix(llm): judge every model answer by the same preconditions
facts.description:
Closes #85
Closes #94

- **One place (#94):** `CallValidity` decides whether a model answer counts, for rephrasing and the thorough check alike. `ChatModel` records the call's usage and hands the answer over; it no longer judges anything itself. A new way for a call to verify nothing is one more precondition in that file.
- **The preconditions, in order:** the whole prompt reached the model (the existing lower bound: characters sent / 8, a count no tokenizer undercuts); the answer reads as the shape asked for; a verdict agrees with itself ("unfaithful" with no claims is not a verdict).
- **Rephrasing is now covered (#85):** a cut prompt fails the rendering as it already failed the check. Before, a truncating endpoint still returned entries written from the facts and rules the model kept. If the cut dropped facts, the audience failed on "no entry for fact N", naming the symptom instead of the cause; if it dropped the middle of the prompt - the rules - the rendering passed.
- **The unparsable path (#76) is folded in,** with its outcome kept: an unreadable verdict is still reported as not evaluated rather than failing the run, since that was decided there and still holds. An unreadable rendering still fails its audience.
- **What cannot be checked is stated in the code** and in `docs/run-metrics.md`: an endpoint that reports the untruncated length, or no usage at all, and a model that saw every fact and judged badly - the reason the rule-based check always runs.
- A truncated call is recorded in the run metrics before it fails: it was paid for.

**Reproduced** as a failing test before the fix (no local endpoint here; the numbers are #85's Ollama run): a rephrase call reporting 4,096 input tokens for a prompt of 600 facts returned entries. After, it fails with `the endpoint reported 4096 input tokens for a prompt of ... characters ... the endpoint's context window is too small for what Chartula sends`.

**Found on the way:** `ChatModelMetricsTests` stubbed 120 input tokens for a 5,606-character customer prompt - a count no tokenizer produces, which the new check rightly rejects. The stub now reports 1,200.

Tests: `ChatModelTests` (a rephrase call that cannot fit its prompt fails naming the context window; a plausible count passes); `ChatModelMetricsTests` (a truncated call is recorded before it fails); `TruncatedEndpointTests` runs the production pipeline against an endpoint reporting 4,096 tokens: every audience fails with the context-window message and nothing is written. The existing faithfulness precondition and not-evaluated tests pass unchanged.

facts.title: feat(serialization): record how changelog.json was made
facts.description:
Closes #179

- `changelog.json` gains an optional `provenance` object with `toolVersion`, `provider`, `model` and `promptHash` (OD18, OD19). It is additive under `schemaVersion: 1`, which the Stability section of `docs/changelog-json.md` allows for a new optional field.
- `toolVersion` is the assembly's informational version, which the SDK already suffixes with the commit it was built from (`0.1.0-alpha+2c43772...`), so the file names the exact build.
- `promptHash` is `sha256:` over every instruction Chartula sends - each audience's system prompt, the thorough check's system prompt and its user template - without the facts, so it changes exactly when a prompt changes. It lives on `ChangelogPromptBuilder.PromptHash`, where #180's snapshot test can use it too.
- A value the run does not have (null or blank) is left out, never written empty; a file written without provenance has no `provenance` key at all. That keeps the stored fixtures byte-identical, so none needed regenerating.
- Endpoint hosts, flags and check verdicts stay out: the file is meant to be published, and a host can name an internal gateway.
- Provenance is assembled in the composition root (`OutputServiceCollectionExtensions.Provenance`) from `LlmOptions` and handed to `FileChangelogJsonWriter`; the pipeline and its port are unchanged.
- `docs/changelog-json.md` documents the object and narrows "fields are always present" to the fields that always were. 

**Verification:** the built binary's informational version reads `0.1.0-alpha+2c43772833e4ed32790e5549848f7f42bc0e4eee`. A full `generate` was not run, since writing `changelog.json` needs a rendering and that costs tokens; the writer, the serializer and the wiring are covered below.

Tests: `ProvenanceSerializationTests` (all four fields written, a null or blank value left out, no provenance means no key, reads back without touching the facts, the prompt hash is a stable SHA-256); `FileChangelogJsonWriterTests` (the written file carries the provenance it was given); `ProvenanceWiringTests` (a run records the tool version, the configured provider and model, and the prompt hash). `FactBaseFixtureTests` pass unchanged, which is the check that files without provenance serialize exactly as before.

facts.title: feat: default to Sonnet 5 and the technical and customer audiences
facts.description:
Closes #177

- **Model (OD14):** the default is `claude-sonnet-5`, named once as `LlmProviderDefaults.AnthropicModel`; `LlmOptions.Model` points at it instead of repeating a literal. A full id, not an alias, so the model cannot move under a run without a change here. This repository's own Sonnet 5 runs cost $0.25-0.29 (`docs/configuration.md`).
- **Audiences (OD15):** a run without `--audience` renders technical and customer - the two with an output of their own (`CHANGELOG.md` and the release notes, `release-<tag>.md`). Product renders only when named: no output file, no evaluation, no named reader, and a third of every run's cost.
- The default lives in the CLI (`AudienceSelection.Default`), where the `--audience` option is read. In the domain `ReleaseRequest.Audiences = null` still means every audience, so the pipeline's contract does not change.
- All three are `--audience technical,customer,product`; the help text, `docs/cli.md` and the README say so. No `all` shorthand, which would be one more name to support for a case the list already covers.
- `docs/configuration.md` marks Sonnet 5 as the default in both tables; `chartula.example.yaml` shows it and names Haiku and Opus 5 as the cheaper and the top tier.
- The thorough-check default is untouched; it is decided after the measurement in #176.

**Verification:** `chartula --help` shows the new `--audience` default. No live run was made, since it costs tokens; which audiences reach the pipeline is decided entirely in `AudienceSelection`, which the tests cover.

Tests: `AudienceSelectionTests` (no option renders technical and customer but not product; all three by naming them), `LlmWiringTests` (with no `llm` section the model is `claude-sonnet-5`).

facts.title: feat: ask where a first release starts instead of rendering all history
facts.description:
Closes #138

- **Decision** (recorded on #138): where a release starts is a fact decision, so the operator makes it. A range that spans all history stops the run; `--since <ref>` names the start, `--whole-history` renders everything on purpose. Not chosen: an automatic cut-off, which would silently decide which changes belong to the release, and detecting superseded changes, which beyond exact reverts means reading meaning - a fact decision in the model.
- The check sits in `ReleasePipeline` right after the commits are read, before the first GitHub request and before the model, so asking costs neither API budget nor tokens. It holds for every mode.
- Core throws `WholeHistoryException` with the tag and the commit count and knows no flags; `ReleaseCommand` turns it into the message with both options. It goes to stdout as `Error: ...`, like every other failure after the pipeline started (`docs/cli.md`, "Exit status").
- `--since` works on any tag and overrides the previous tag. `GitCliCommitReader` verifies the ref resolves to a commit and is an ancestor of the release tag (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`), otherwise the range would hold commits that are not in the release.
- `CommitRange.FromTag` becomes `From` and `IsFirstRelease` becomes `IsWholeHistory`: the start can now be a commit, and a first tag with `--since` is not a whole-history range. Neither is serialized, so `changelog.json` is unchanged.
- Passing both options, or `--since` without a value, is refused before configuration is read.
- `docs/cli.md` gets "Where a release starts", including the remaining limitation that a change replaced later in the same range is still its own entry; the README usage shows both options. The README's known-limitations line goes in with #182 (noted there).

**Repro and verification** on this repository, whose first tag is `v0.1.0-preview.1`: before, `chartula preview --tag v0.1.0-preview.1` rendered 48 entries from 69 commits (the #95 run). After:

```
Error: v0.1.0-preview.1 is the first tag, so its range is the whole history (69 commits).
  Rendered as it is, that reads as a development log rather than a release.
  --since <ref>     start the release after a tag or commit (e.g. the last state you shipped)
  --whole-history   render all of it, e.g. for a project whose history is the release
```

exit 1, no request made. An unresolvable `--since` and passing both options fail with their own messages. A full run with `--since` was not made, since it costs tokens; the range it reads is covered by the reader tests.

Tests: `WholeHistoryTests` (a first tag without a start throws before GitHub and the model, enforced by stand-ins that throw if reached; `WholeHistory` renders; `Since` reaches the reader); `GitCliCommitReaderTests` (a named start bounds a first tag, overrides the previous tag and accepts a commit expression, an unresolvable or non-ancestor start is refused); `ReleaseStartTests` (parsing, both refused, missing value refused, help names both, the refusal names cause and both ways out); `FirstTagTests` runs the built CLI in a checkout whose only tag is its first. `CliProcess` now returns stdout as well.

facts.title: fix(curation): read no description from hidden comments or an unfilled template
facts.description:
Closes #141

- **Decision: both.** HTML comments are stripped from every body, and a body with nothing left but headings and checklist items is treated as absent. Comments alone would not be enough: #73's template keeps its headings and ticked boxes once the comments are gone.
- Comments go from every body, not only template-shaped ones: GitHub does not render them, so nobody reading the pull request saw them, and the template's comments are exactly where its examples sit. An unterminated `` linked issue #123 to the change, and a comment containing `BREAKING CHANGE:` would have flagged it as breaking, because categorization reads the description too.
- A body with anything besides headings and boxes is kept as written, headings and boxes included: curation removes what the author did not say, it does not edit what they did.
- `PullRequestBody` lives in `Curation` and runs once in `ReleaseChangeResolver`, so the title fallback, breaking status, linked issues and the prompt all read the same description. Deterministic, `[GeneratedRegex]`, no model involved.
- `docs/changelog-json.md` says when `description` is `null` now. Type and nullability are unchanged, so no schema version bump; the stored fixtures are fact bases downstream of curation and do not change.

**Reproduced** as a failing test before the fix (a live run costs tokens): #73's body verbatim became the description, and the fact built from a body with the template's comments carried `LinkedIssues: [123]`.

**Checked against real data:** the bodies of all 82 merged pull requests in this repository went through the resolver. Exactly two lose their description, #73 and #105, both the untouched template; every other body keeps its text.

Tests: `ReleaseChangeResolverTests` (#73's body yields no description and does not stand in for an uninformative title, a filled template keeps its text without placeholders, comments stripped inline, multi-line and unterminated, heading- and checklist-only bodies absent, prose with headings and boxes kept verbatim); `FactBaseBuilderTests` (a template comment links no issue and flags nothing as breaking).

facts.title: docs(repo): add a security policy with private reporting
facts.description:
Closes #161

- `SECURITY.md` names GitHub private vulnerability reporting as the channel and asks not to open a public issue. Private reporting is now enabled on the repository (`PUT /repos/goldbarth/chartula/private-vulnerability-reporting`, done by hand - it is a setting, not part of the diff).
- Supported versions: alpha, no stable release; fixes go to `main` and the next preview. That is what exists today - `v0.1.0` is still a draft.
- Response targets are stated as targets for a one-person project: acknowledgement within 3 working days, assessment within 14, fix or plan agreed before disclosure, credit in the advisory.
- Scope is drawn around what the reviews found to matter: repository content or a setting the operator did not choose reaching a credential, running a program, writing where the run was not asked to, or a credential landing in output. An unfaithful rendering, an unexposed dependency issue, or a precondition of a compromised operator machine go to normal issues instead.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` says a vulnerability is the exception to "open an issue"; `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml` adds a "Report a security vulnerability" link to the issue chooser, with blank issues left enabled.

**Verification:** `GET /repos/goldbarth/chartula/private-vulnerability-reporting` answers `{"enabled":true}`; the advisory link in `SECURITY.md` resolves (redirects to sign-in when logged out).

Tests: none, documentation and repository settings only.

facts.title: docs(cli): recommend a fine-grained token instead of gh auth token
facts.description:
Closes #160

- `docs/cli.md` gets a "A GitHub token" section: a fine-grained personal access token scoped to the one repository, with a permission table derived from the two kinds of request Chartula makes - `GET commits/{sha}/pulls` (Contents and Pull requests, read-only) and the releases endpoints for the draft (Contents, read and write; listing drafts needs push access anyway). Metadata is listed because GitHub adds it to every fine-grained token.
- A read-only token is named as the safer default until publishing, since `preview` and `--no-publish` never write.
- `gh auth token` stays documented as a local shortcut, with the trade-off named: it is the GitHub CLI's OAuth token, typically `repo` scope, read and write to every repository the user can reach - handed to a process that reads repository content.
- The README drops the `gh auth token` line and links to the section.
- `GitHubTokenNotice` points to `https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new` with the permissions and `export <variable>=<token>`, still naming the variable as configured.

**Verification:** the notice as printed by a run without `GITHUB_TOKEN`:

```
Warning: no GitHub token found in GITHUB_TOKEN - the run continues unauthenticated.
  GitHub allows 60 requests an hour per IP address without one, and a run
  spends roughly one per pull request, so a release can exhaust the budget
  partway through. A token raises the limit to 5000.
  Create a fine-grained token for this repository at https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new
  with Contents and Pull requests read-only (Contents read and write to publish
  release notes), then: export GITHUB_TOKEN=<token>
```

The permission table follows GitHub's REST reference for the two endpoints; it was not exercised with a real fine-grained token for this PR.

Tests: `GitHubTokenNoticeTests` asserts the notice names a fine-grained token and the creation URL, and no longer mentions `gh auth token`.

facts.title: fix(config): require https for every endpoint except loopback
facts.description:
Closes #159

- `EndpointUrl.Require` is the one check for every configured endpoint: an absolute `https` URL, or `http` to a loopback host (`Uri.IsLoopback`: `localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`). Anything else is refused with a message that names the variable, the value and the rule (OD2: strictest and simplest; a private-range exception would leave the same path open on a shared network).
- Applied where the settings are read, so a bad URL is refused before any work starts: `Chartula__GitHub__ApiBaseUrl` in `GitHubHttpClientFactory.ReadOptions`, `Chartula__Llm__BaseUrl` in `LlmServiceCollectionExtensions.ReadOptions` for both providers - a proxy in front of the Anthropic API receives the key as much as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint does.
- The OpenAI-compatible client's own scheme check (http or https to anywhere) is replaced by the shared one. Its "localhost:11434 is not a URL" case keeps working, now at startup instead of at client creation.
- `LlmOptions.BaseUrlVariable` and `GitHubOptions.ApiBaseUrlVariable` name the variables once, for the yaml refusal and the error messages.
- `docs/configuration.md` states the rule under "Environment-only settings".

**Repro:** `Chartula__GitHub__ApiBaseUrl=http://example.invalid/ chartula preview --tag v0.1.0 --repo owner/name`. Before: the run started and failed on DNS (`Could not reach the GitHub API ... example.invalid:80`), so a reachable host would have received the token over http; the same held for `Chartula__Llm__BaseUrl`. After: both exit 1 with `Configuration error: ... uses http to another machine, which would send credentials in cleartext.` `http://localhost:11434/v1` for a local model still starts.

Tests: `EndpointUrlTests` (https anywhere and http to loopback accepted; http to public, private and `0.0.0.0` hosts and to `localhost.example.com` refused; non-URLs refused); `LlmWiringTests` refuses http to another machine for both providers at startup; `InsecureEndpointTests` runs the built CLI with an http GitHub endpoint and asserts it stops before any request.

facts.title: fix(config): read endpoints and credential names from the environment only
facts.description:
Closes #158

- `chartula.yaml` may no longer set `llm.baseUrl`, `llm.apiKeyEnvironmentVariable`, `github.apiBaseUrl` or `github.tokenEnvironmentVariable`. The file is repository content, and these four decide where release data and credentials are sent. A file that sets one is refused at startup rather than ignored, and the message names the `Chartula__` variable to use instead, so nobody believes a setting is in force that is not (OD1: no opt-in flag).
- The process environment is no longer loaded whole. `ChartulaConfiguration` reads `Chartula__*` settings plus the credential variables Chartula uses: both providers' default key names, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and whatever the two name settings point at. Those name settings can only come from the environment now, so no repository value can make an arbitrary variable readable (R03).
- Every run prints the endpoints and credential variable names in force to stderr, never values (`EndpointNotice`). An environment is easy to inherit without reading it - a shell profile, a CI runner.
- Error messages of the OpenAI-compatible provider name `Chartula__Llm__BaseUrl` instead of `llm.baseUrl`.
- `docs/configuration.md` gets an "Environment-only settings" section; the local and hosted OpenAI-compatible examples, `docs/cli.md` and `chartula.example.yaml` move the four settings to the environment. This breaks a `chartula.yaml` that sets them; the refusal says how to fix it.

**Repro:** a checkout whose `chartula.yaml` sets `github.apiBaseUrl: http://127.0.0.1:8765/` and `github.tokenEnvironmentVariable: SOME_OTHER_SECRET`, a local listener on that port, then `SOME_OTHER_SECRET=topsecret chartula preview --tag v0.1.0 --repo owner/name`. Before: the listener received `Authorization: Bearer topsecret`. After: the run exits 1 before any request, naming `Chartula__GitHub__ApiBaseUrl` and `Chartula__GitHub__TokenEnvironmentVariable`. The same two values set in the environment still work, and the run names them first.

Tests: `ChartulaYamlConfigurationTests` (each of the four keys refused naming its variable, all named at once); `ChartulaConfigurationTests` (an unrelated variable is not readable, default and renamed credentials are, environment overrides the file); `EndpointNoticeTests` (defaults and overrides, no values); `RepositoryConfigurationTests` runs the built CLI against the repro `chartula.yaml`. `LlmWiringTests` and `GitHubTokenNoticeTests` now build configuration the way `Program` does and set endpoints and names in the environment. The process helper from `PlantedGitTests` moved to `CliProcess`.

facts.title: fix(history): resolve git from PATH, never from the checkout
facts.description:
Closes #157

- `GitExecutable` resolves `git` (`git.exe` on Windows) once to an absolute path from `PATH`. Started by bare name, .NET's `Process` looks in the application directory and the current directory first, and a run's current directory is the checkout it reads - so a committed `git` ran with the operator's environment, keys included, on every OS.
- Relative `PATH` entries (`.`, an empty entry) are skipped: they resolve against the current directory, which is the hole being closed. On Unix a candidate must carry an execute bit.
- Resolved in `AddChartulaHistory` rather than on first use, so a machine without git is refused before any work starts, with a message that names `PATH`. Every reader runs the same binary.
- `GitCliRepositoryReader` comes from the composition root; `Program` no longer constructs it (R99).

**Repro:** a checkout with an executable `./git` that writes `$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` to a file, then `chartula preview --tag v0.1.0 --repo owner/name` from it. Before: the file holds the key. After: no file, the real git resolves the tag and the run goes on to GitHub.

Tests: `GitExecutableTests` (first match wins, relative entries skipped, non-executable skipped, empty `PATH` fails naming it); `PlantedGitTests` runs the built CLI from a checkout with a planted git (a shell script on Unix, a copy of `whoami.exe` on Windows) and fails against the old `FileName = "git"`. Existing reader tests pass the resolved git.

facts.title: fix(output): keep a draft attached to its tag when its notes are updated
facts.description:
Follow-up to #154 (#131), found while verifying it against the live API and committed after the merge, so it is its own PR.

- `UpdateReleaseRequest` carries `tag_name`. GitHub detaches a draft from its tag when a PATCH leaves the tag out (`tag_name` becomes `untagged-...`), so the next run could not find the draft and would create another one. The update sends the tag it already has.
- The comment on `FindDraftByTagAsync` states the remaining window: the release list lags a new release by a moment, so two runs for the same tag started seconds apart can still leave two drafts. A run takes longer than that.

Tests: the existing "updates an existing draft" case now asserts `tag_name` is in the PATCH body.

Behaviour was confirmed against the live API before the commit (`goldbarth/port-tidewatch`, temporary tag): a second run updates the one draft, tag kept, body replaced. Nothing was re-run against the live API for this PR.

facts.title: feat(output): create release notes as a draft
facts.description:
Closes #131

- `CreateReleaseRequest` sends `draft: true`; a new release is always a draft.
- An existing release is updated with the body only (PATCH), so a published release stays published and a draft stays a draft.
- `GET /releases/tags/{tag}` answers published releases only. When it finds nothing, the writer pages through `GET /releases` (drafts are listed for a token with push access, which writing needs anyway) and updates a draft for the tag, so re-running does not stack drafts.
- The returned link is marked `(draft)`, so `Wrote:` says there is a step left.
- README and `docs/cli.md` describe the draft.

Tests: new release created as draft, existing draft found in the list and updated, published release updated without a draft field.

**Verified against the live API** on `goldbarth/port-tidewatch` with a temporary tag (release, draft and tag deleted afterwards), running the real writer:

- First run creates a draft; the lookup by tag answers 404 for it, the release list has it.
- Found there: a PATCH without `tag_name` detaches a draft from its tag (`tag_name` becomes `untagged-...`), so the next run could not find it. The update now sends the tag. After the fix, a second run updates the one draft, tag kept, body replaced.
- The list lags a new release by a few seconds; two runs started that close together can still leave two drafts. Stated in the code.
- A draft's `html_url` changes on every update; the published release for `v1.3.0` was not touched.

facts.title: fix(cli): exit non-zero when a requested audience failed
facts.description:
Closes #148

Decisions from the issue's open question:

- **Partial failure exits 1.** Every requested audience is part of the result; what rendered is still written, and the output says `<n> of <m> audiences failed.`
- **Nothing rendered, nothing written.** `ReleasePipeline` skips the write step when no audience rendered, so an earlier `changelog.json` is not replaced by one without renderings.

Output headers: `No changelog generated for <tag>: no audience rendered.` / `No preview for <tag>: no audience rendered.` instead of `Generated` / `Preview`.

`docs/cli.md` exit status updated.

**Repro and verification:** `generate --no-publish` in a clone of `goldbarth/port-tidewatch` with an invalid `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and an existing `changelog.json`. Before: `Generated changelog`, exit 0, file overwritten. After: `No changelog generated`, `Nothing to write.`, exit 1, file untouched. `preview` likewise exits 1.

Tests: pipeline writes nothing when all failed and writes what rendered on partial failure; command exit codes and headers for all, partial and no success.

facts.title: fix(llm): refuse an anthropic run without a key before any work starts
facts.description:
Closes #147

- `AddChartulaLlm` refuses `llm.provider: anthropic` when the configured key variable is empty, naming the variable (renamed or default) and how to set it. Reported as `Configuration error: ...`, exit 1.
- Checked after the other configuration refusals, so a wrong `chartula.yaml` value is named first.
- `openai-compatible` is untouched: a local server needs no key.
- `Program`: configuration is built before the release target is resolved, so a config error comes before any git read; the GitHub token warning now follows the target resolution.
- `docs/cli.md` Environment section shows the refusal.

**Repro and verification:** `chartula preview` in a clone of `goldbarth/port-tidewatch` without `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Before: tag and repo resolved, pull requests fetched, raw `401` JSON per audience. After: the one-line configuration error, exit 1, no GitHub request.

Tests: missing key refused, renamed variable named, openai-compatible starts without a key; existing wiring tests now supply a key.

facts.title: feat(cli): default --tag and --repo from the checkout the run starts in
facts.description:
Closes #150

`cd my-repo && chartula preview` now runs with no flags.

- `--tag` defaults to the nearest tag reachable from `HEAD`, `--repo` to owner/name from the `origin` remote (`https://`, `ssh://`, `git@host:`, with or without `.git`, host not checked so GitHub Enterprise works).
- Both flags still override; a malformed `--repo` is refused, not replaced by the remote.
- A defaulted value is announced on stderr before the run, so `generate` never publishes to a release the user did not see.
- A default that cannot be read fails before any network call, naming the option and the directory.
- `GitCli` extracted from `GitCliCommitReader` so the new `GitCliRepositoryReader` shares the process handling.
- Help text, README usage, `docs/cli.md` updated.

**Verified end to end** in `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0` against a clone of `goldbarth/port-tidewatch`: no flags (https remote), ssh remote, no remote, explicit flags without remote, repository without tags, outside any git repository.

Tests: remote URL parsing (8 accepted, 5 refused forms), resolution and messages, and the git reads against real temporary repositories.

facts.title: fix(generation): escape angle brackets the model writes outside code spans
facts.description:
Closes #137

- `RenderingComposer.EscapeAngleBrackets` escapes every `<` outside a code span in the entry text and the customer label the model wrote. The plan's reference and markers are not touched.
- Code spans follow CommonMark: closed by a backtick run of the same length; an unmatched run is literal text. An already escaped `\<` is left as it is.
- Applies to all three audiences, so `CHANGELOG.md`, release notes and `release-<tag>.md` all get it. The customer description (YAML front matter) is not Markdown and stays unescaped.
- Repro first: a fixture pipeline test pushes `release-<tag>.md` through the real composer; it failed for every audience before the fix.

**Decision on #137's open question:** escaping in code for correctness, deterministic and not skippable by the model. Formatting identifiers as code is a prompt matter and split off into #143.

The committed `CHANGELOG.md` still shows `release-.md` until it is regenerated with #37.

facts.title: fix(faithfulness): ground the pull request reference the thorough check sees
facts.description:
Closes #140

- `ThoroughFaithfulnessChecker.ToGroundedFacts` now adds `(pull request #N, url)` to each statement with a pull request, the link alone when there is no number, nothing for a commit-based change.
- Repro first: a fixture pipeline test hands the real composed technical rendering to a recording model and asserts every `[#N](url)` in it appears in the facts the check received. Failed before the fix on `typical-release` and `breaking-release`.
- Two unit tests pin the statement shape with and without a pull request.

Not verified against a live model (costs tokens). The run from #95 with `thinking: disabled` is the case that would show 48 flags dropping to the real ones.

facts.title: docs: add the changelog Chartula generated for itself
facts.description:
Closes #95

- `CHANGELOG.md` generated by Chartula for a local, unpushed `v0.1.0-preview.1` tag and committed as written.
- Run: `generate --tag v0.1.0-preview.1 --repo goldbarth/chartula --audience technical --no-publish`, provider `anthropic`, model `claude-sonnet-5`, thinking `provider-default` (same settings as the eval runs), 0.29 USD.

Only the note was added by hand; entries are untouched.

**Findings**

- #137 identifiers written as prose; GitHub strips `<tag>` from `release-<tag>.md`
- #138 first release renders the whole history, superseded changes included
- #140 thorough check flags every PR reference as unsupported (48 false claims with thinking disabled)

facts.title: feat: put the structure of every rendering together in code
facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

Moves the structure of every rendering out of the prompt and into code.
The model now writes the words of each entry and nothing else.

- The model is sent the facts with an id each and answers with one text per id, as structured output (`RenderedEntries`).
- `GroundedFactsFactory` plans each audience before the call: which changes, in which order, under which group, whether breaking, and a technical entry's reference.
- `RenderingComposer` writes the headings, the `**Breaking:**` marker, the customer label and the reference around those texts.
- A fact left without an entry, answered twice, or an entry for a fact that was never sent fails that audience with a message naming the ids, instead of vanishing from the rendering.
- The prompts lose every structure rule and keep the rules for how an entry is worded.
- The customer description is a field of the answer, so `ReleaseDescription` is removed.

Groups per audience:

| Audience | Groups, in order |
|---|---|
| Technical | Changed, Added, Fixed - breaking first within each |
| Customer | What needs action (breaking, or labelled `labels.actionRequired`), What's New, What's Changed, Bug Fixes |
| Product | Other |

There is no collapsed `Also:` line any more: every change gets its own entry.

Two commits, each builds and passes on its own:

| Commit | Change |
|---|---|
| `feat(labels): a label for a change the reader has to act on` | `labels.actionRequired`, carried by `LabelRules` |
| `feat(generation): put the structure of every rendering together in code` | the plan, the structured answer, the composer, the prompts, tests and docs |

Unchanged: the `changelog.json` schema, review, both faithfulness checks, the written files.

## Why?

#96: five renderings of one release on four models came back in five structures while the prompt still carried format rules, two of them from the same model.
Under the decision rule for the alpha, a structure that is not identical across runs moves into code.
See the comparison on #96.

## Verified

`dotnet build Chartula.slnx -c Release`: 0 warnings, 0 errors, on both commits.
`dotnet test Chartula.slnx -c Release`: 462 passing on the last commit (Core 352, Infrastructure 33, Cli 77).

One live run of this branch, 2026-09-16: `claude-sonnet-5`, `v0.1.0` as tagged today (`0d4f6f4`, 44 changes), all audiences, `--no-publish`.
No audience failed, and the structure matches the plan exactly:

| | Entries | Groups | Lines that are not entries |
|---|---|---|---|
| Technical | 38 of 38 | Added 31, Fixed 7 | 0 |
| Customer | 35 of 35 | What's New 28, Bug Fixes 7 | 0 |
| Product | 38 of 38 | Other 38 | 0 |

All 38 technical entries end on their reference and all 35 customer entries carry a label.
The customer page carries its description, and `CHANGELOG.md` opens on `## 0.1.0 - 2026-09-04`.

## Observed, not resolved here

- **Tokens and cost.** 95,400 in / 33,887 out for rephrasing and 113,190 in / 24,943 out for the thorough check, about $1.51 at list prices. That is roughly double the earlier Sonnet runs. Part of it is the larger range - 44 changes where those runs had 28 - and part is this change: every fact now gets its own entry, the customer entries carry a label, and the answer is JSON. The two were not separated; that would take another run on `8061f46`.
- **Duration.** The run took 10 minutes 1 second, where earlier runs took two to three. The cause is unknown: the run records neither the time per call nor retries by the provider client. That is #128.
- **`openai-compatible` endpoints** that do not honour the JSON schema now fail the rendering rather than returning free text.

Closes #96
Refs #128

facts.title: feat: give every audience the shape its template and rubric specify
facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

Brings all three audience prompts in line with the templates and rubrics finished in [chartula-evals](https://github.com/goldbarth/chartula-evals).
What a template decides rather than words is set when the facts are built, never in a prompt.

Four commits, each builds and passes on its own:

| Commit | Change |
|---|---|
| `fix(prompting): take the customer rules from the rubric they are judged by` | The customer rules no longer contradict `rubric/customer.md` or each other, and close on two finished example entries |
| `feat(output): open a CHANGELOG.md release on its version and date` | `## 1.2.0 - 2026-06-14` instead of `## v1.2.0`; sections under the old heading are still matched |
| `feat(generation): hand the model what a template decides as facts` | Selection, technical group and reference, and product theme are decided in `GroundedFactsFactory` |
| `feat(prompting): give the technical and product renderings their templates` | The technical and product prompts carry the rules of their templates |

## Why?

#122: the customer outcome rule was a test that rejects a sentence and does not produce one.
Reading every rule against the rubric found more: "stop once the outcome is stated" cut off the action the rubric places after it, and "always written" left the model to invent an outcome the facts do not give.

#96: technical and product stated tone only, so their structure was whatever the model chose.
Their templates now exist, Common Changelog for technical and thematic for product.

## What a reader will see change

- Technical and product no longer carry docs, internal work or refactors, unless a label brings them in or the change is breaking.
- Technical entries are grouped Changed, Added, Fixed, with a breaking change first in its group.
- Product entries all stand under `Other` until a label allowlist exists.
- `CHANGELOG.md` sections open on `## VERSION - DATE`.

## Not covered

- Authors on technical entries: the fact base carries none.
- The Removed group: nothing marks a change as a removal.

## Verified

`dotnet build Chartula.slnx -c Release`: 0 warnings, 0 errors, on every commit.
`dotnet test Chartula.slnx -c Release`: 455 passing on the last commit (Core 346, Infrastructure 33, Cli 76).
No run against a live model was made; rendering and judging come after this PR.

Refs #122, #96

facts.title: fix(prompting): say where an outcome comes from, not only what is not one
facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

The outcome rule in `CustomerFormat` gains a first half that says where the
sentence comes from. The test that was there stays and becomes the check on what
that half produced.

```diff
+ - Write what the reader can now rely on from their side of the change,
+ not from the change: what they no longer have to do, no longer have to
+ check, no longer have to work around, or can now count on without looking.
+ For a fix it is never that the fault is gone - the fault is the opening,
+ and the outcome is what the reader no longer has to do about it. Take it
+ from the facts of this change, which usually say what it was for.
  - The outcome must survive this test: strike the opening clause and read
  what is left. If it only restates the opening, negates it, or names a value
  or a mechanism, it is not an outcome. ...
```

## Why?

Ten of the 24 entries of the customer rendering of 2026-09-08 say what changed
and never what the reader gets from it. Nine of them fail nothing else, so this
one shape is the difference between 11 entries shipping and 20.

The test was already in the prompt when those entries were written. A test
rejects a sentence and does not produce one: a model that has written the
mechanism keeps the mechanism, because nothing has said what the sentence should
have been. Three of the ten, verbatim:

```
- **Configuration errors**: A mistake in `chartula.yaml` now stops the run with
  a plain `Configuration error: ...` message instead of an unhandled exception.

- **Fallback for missing PR data**: When a release has no associated pull
  requests, ... the changelog now falls back to the commit message or the pull
  request's description instead of leaving that change out.

- **Grouped by pull request**: Changes are now summarized per merged pull
  request rather than per raw commit, using each pull request's title,
  description, and labels.
```

The first two close on the negation of their own opening; the third never leaves
the mechanism.

Refs #122

## The material is in the fact base, which is why this is a prompt change

Each of the nine entries that fail on this and nothing else was held against
`test-runs/v0.1.0-facts.md` in
[chartula-evals](https://github.com/goldbarth/chartula-evals) on 2026-09-09.
Eight of the nine have their outcome in the facts they were written from:

| Entry | The outcome, in the facts |
|---|---|
| Configuration errors | the run stops at startup rather than partway, and the message names the valid values |
| Fallback for missing PR data | "never hard-fails solely because PR discipline is imperfect" |
| Configuration file | "A present config refines behavior; it is never required" |

The exception is the entry about linked issues, where the facts say the closing
keywords are parsed and nothing about what a reader gets from it. One of nine,
and nothing here changes how that case is rendered.

`dotnet build Chartula.slnx -c Release`: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
`dotnet test Chartula.slnx -c Release`: 433 passing (Core 324, Infrastructure
33, Cli 76), one of them new -
`Says_where_an_outcome_is_taken_from_before_testing_the_one_written`.

harness, over three renderings, per the turn budget in its `pipeline.md`.

facts.title: fix(facts): decide what a reader can meet from a label, not from a category
facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

`IsUserVisible` stops being a property of the category.

```diff
- private static bool IsUserVisible(ChangeCategory category, bool isBreaking)
-     => isBreaking || category is ChangeCategory.Feature ...
+ private static bool IsUserVisible(ChangeCategory category, bool isBreaking, bool? labelled)
+     => isBreaking || (labelled ?? IsOutwardFacingCategory(category));
```

`LabelDecision` carries what the labels say: `true`, `false`, or `null` when they
say nothing - silence is not a "no". The names come from `chartula.yaml`:

```yaml
labels:
  internal: [visibility:internal]
  userFacing: [visibility:user-facing]
```

## Why?

Everything typed `feat:` was user-visible by definition - on v0.1.0 of this
repository, 26 of 28 changes, the serialisation format and the layout of the
written files among them. The customer prompt carries every fact it is handed,
so it wrote about them because it was asked to.

A category says what kind of change something is, not whether a reader can meet
one. Nor does a scope: `output` holds both `store all audience texts in
changelog.json` and `write CHANGELOG.md`. A label is the only signal that
answers the question, and a person answers it while writing the pull request.

Closes #119

## Verified against v0.1.0 of this repository

Six pull requests were labelled, then a real run produced this fact base:

```
hidden  | visibility:internal    | feat(output): store all audience texts in changelog.json
hidden  | visibility:internal    | feat(formatting): consistent formatting and tone per audience
hidden  | visibility:internal    | feat(serialization): write the fact base to changelog.json
visible | visibility:user-facing | feat(rendering): render technical, customer, and PM from one fact base
visible | visibility:user-facing | feat(facts): make fact-base depth configurable
visible | visibility:user-facing | feat(prompting): prompt architecture that rephrases facts, never invents
```

Unlabelled changes fell back to their category unchanged: `docs:` and
`refactor(prompting):` hidden, every `feat:` visible. All eight acceptance
criteria hold.

## Notes for review

- **An internal label wins over a user-facing one** on the same change. The two
  together are a contradiction a person wrote, and that reading cannot put an
  internal change in front of a reader.
- **Labelling nothing changes nothing.** With no visibility labels configured the
  category decides, as it always has - the existing suite passes untouched.
- **`LabelWiringTests` goes from YAML text to `LabelRules`.** That is the seam
  where a name the composition root forgets to pass on becomes a rule that is
  configured, read, and then ignored.
- **`chartula.yaml` declares the two names**, because `visibility:internal` is
  this repository's convention and another project writes `internal`,

facts.title: feat(facts): carry the labels of a change into the fact base
facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

`ChangeFact` carries the labels of the change, and `changelog.json` writes them.

```diff
  IReadOnlyList<int> LinkedIssues,
+ IReadOnlyList<string> Labels,
  string? Description)
```

```diff
  "linkedIssues": [12],
+ "labels": ["area:ui"],
  "description": "Adds a dark theme toggle."
```

They arrive verbatim and unfiltered, the ones curation acted on included: which
labels an output shows is that output's decision, and a fact the base drops
cannot be recovered further down. A commit carries no labels, so a commit-based
change gets an empty list rather than a null.

## Why?

`ReleaseChange` has the labels and `LabelRulePolicy` already reads them during
curation, but they stopped there.

Today that is a gap. It becomes a blocker the moment a rendering wants subject
matter in the output - tags on a customer release page, a filter on a site,
grouping by topic rather than by change type. The fact base is the only source a
rendering may draw from, so a label that never reaches it cannot be rendered,
and a tag invented outside it is exactly what the rule-based check flags as a
name the facts do not support.

The decision behind it is written up in goldbarth/chartula-evals
`docs/output-format.md`, section Tags: tags come from pull request labels, never
from the categories and never from a fixed vocabulary.

Closes #98

## Notes for review

- **The field sits between `LinkedIssues` and `Description`.** Both are
  collections of the change's own metadata; the free text stays at the end. That
  breaks every positional call site, which is the point - the compiler listed all
  14 rather than letting one slide through.
- **Labels are compared by content**, like the linked issues, order included. A
  record compares a list by reference, and two facts holding the same labels in
  different instances are one fact.
- **`schemaVersion` stays 1.** An optional field is non-breaking per the
  documented contract in `docs/changelog-json.md`. A document written before the
  field existed reads back with no labels rather than with a null the rest of the
  pipeline would have to guard against - as a test rather than as a claim.
- **The fixtures carry the field.** `typical-release` got real labels,
  `commits-only-release` empty lists, and the byte comparison against what the
  writer produces is green, so they still represent real runs.
- **Nothing in the rendering path changed.** `GroundedFactsFactory` and the
  prompts are untouched: this is the fact, not its use. The allowlist deciding
  which labels reach an output belongs to the output-format work.
- **#119 depends on this.** It needs a signal for user-visibility that the
  category cannot give, and a label is the only one that answers the question
  being asked. It is not in here.

facts.title: fix(llm): put the place a setting is reached behind the outcome
facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

One sentence in the customer prompt, connecting two rules that did not know
about each other.

```
  - If an entry offers the reader a setting or a decision, say where it is
  set, as a place they can find rather than as a key.
+ That place is the fourth part of the entry, so it comes after what the reader
+ can now rely on and never instead of it: an entry that ends on where something
+ is set has not said what setting it gets them.
  If the facts do not say where, leave the option out rather than announce it
  with no place.
```

## Why?

An entry has four parts in order: what the reader observes, who it applies to,
what they can now rely on, what they have to do. Entries about a setting had the
first and the fourth, and nothing in between:

```
- **Fact-base depth**: You can control how much source material feeds each
  change's description - title only, title plus pull request description (the
  default), or title, description, and linked issues. This is set in the
  factBase section of `chartula.yaml`.
```

What does choosing one get the reader? The entry does not say, and the rule
asking for the place was being followed rather than broken: nothing said the
place is the fourth part, so it was written where the third belongs.

Five of the ten outcome failures in the rendering of 2026-09-04 are that shape -
`s5r-01`, `s5r-10`, `s5r-14`, `s5r-15`, `s5r-16` in goldbarth/chartula-evals,
judged by `labelled-all-claude-sonnet-5-2026-09-04T142930.json`.

- **The rest of the rule is untouched.** The place is still named as a place and
  not as a key, and an option whose place the facts do not carry is still left
  out rather than announced without one.
- **The other five failures are not in here.** They are entries about a fix
  closing on the negation of their own opening, which needs a different sentence.
  Both halves land on the same count, and two changes to one count in one turn
  cannot be told apart afterwards - which is why this is one sentence and not

facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

`--audience` names what a run renders. Repeat it or separate the names with
commas; without it all three are rendered, exactly as before.

```bash
chartula generate --tag v1.2.0 --repo owner/name --audience customer
chartula generate --tag v1.2.0 --repo owner/name --audience technical,product
```

An output whose audience was not rendered is not written: no `CHANGELOG.md`
without the technical rendering, no `release-<tag>.md` without the customer one.
That is not a new rule - the pipeline already writes each output only when the
rendering it is made of is present.

An unknown name is an error that lists the three that exist:

```
Unknown audience 'custmer'. There are three: technical, customer, product.
```

## Why?

Each audience is a rephrasing call and a faithfulness check of its own, and the
fact base behind all three is identical. A run that measures one audience's
wording paid for two renderings nobody read, on every render.

That is not only tidiness. The evaluation loop in goldbarth/chartula-evals is
what says whether a change to the customer prompt was an improvement; it is paid

measuring run answered a question nobody asked.

facts.title: fix(llm): leave the model room to write after it has finished thinking
facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

Raises `maxOutputTokens` from 16,000 to 32,000, in the core options, in the CLI
configuration default and in `docs/configuration.md`. One change, nothing else.

Thinking is produced against this ceiling and goes first, which the option's
documentation now says.

## Why?

Four of the five renders on 2026-09-04 wrote a customer rendering of zero
characters and no `release-<tag>.md`, and reported no error. Technical and
product were fine in all of them.

Chartula's own request was captured off the wire during a `preview` run pointed
at a local stand-in for the API, then sent to the real API unchanged:

```
model claude-sonnet-5 | max_tokens 16000 | thinking None
system 4951 chars | messages [('user', 46649)]

  stop_reason : max_tokens
  usage       : in 18527, out 16000
  blocks      : ['thinking']
  TEXT        : 0 chars
```

Exactly the ceiling, a thinking block, and no text block at all.

Only the customer audience is affected because it is the only one whose shape is
specified, and so the only one with a long prompt:

| Audience | System prompt |
| --- | --- |
| Technical | 751 characters |
| Product | 699 characters |
| Customer | 4,951 characters |

The same call against the shorter customer prompt of 4,136 characters used
13,755 of the 16,000 and did return text, 6,133 characters of it. The call has
been sitting just under the ceiling for a while; #112 added four format rules
and pushed it over.

32,000 is twice the current value: thinking wants 12,000 to over 16,000 here and
the text another 1,500 to 6,000, so this leaves the text as much room as the
thinking rather than moving the edge a little further up.

Closes #113

## Notes for review

- **Two defaults, both moved.** `ChatModelOptions` carries the core default and
  `LlmOptions` the configured one; the composition root reads the second and
  hands it to the first, so leaving either behind would have left the effective
  value unchanged or the two disagreeing.
- **The trade-off is a longer wait.** The ceiling's own note says it stays under
  the HTTP timeout a non-streaming request is subject to. That note is why this
  is a doubling and not a tenfold rise. If a timeout does appear it will appear
  as an error rather than as an empty field, which is the better failure of the
  two.
- **Deliberately not in here:** `ChatModel.RephraseAsync` returns `response.Text`
  without looking at `FinishReason` or at whether the response carried any text.
  That is what let four renders lose an entire audience and exit cleanly, and it
  is a defect worth its own change - but it repairs nothing, and shipping it
  alongside this would leave the next render unable to say which of the two
  worked.

facts.title: feat(llm): carry the four format rules the customer prompt left out
facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

Four rules of the customer output format now reach the model. They were written
down, they are judged, and the prompt did not carry them.

```
+ Every entry that asks something of the reader stands above every entry that
+ does not, whichever group each of them sits in. One such entry below one that
+ asks nothing is wrong even when the groups themselves are in order. A breaking
+ change comes first of all.
+ Nothing follows the last group. A migration link belongs in its entry, not in
+ a closing line.

+ Changes the reader would not act on are gathered into one closing bullet of
+ their group, opening with "Also:", rather than each taking a bullet of its
+ own. That bullet is one entry and carries the observation alone: the three
+ parts below do not apply to it.

+ A claim of degree - faster, smaller, higher, more reliable - needs something
+ in the entry the reader can check it against. Without a number or a basis,
+ leave the claim out rather than soften it.
```

Each is pinned by a test, as the rules around them are.

## Why?

Measured on the rendering of 2026-09-04, judged against the frozen customer
criterion in goldbarth/chartula-evals. Two of the four failed that document:

- An entry saying separate marketing files are no longer written, which costs a
  reader who relies on them, sat below entries that ask nothing.
- "defaults to a much higher value" is a claim of degree with nothing to check
  it against. The rule next to it forbids superlatives and marketing language,
  and that phrase is neither, so it passed.

A document axis failing makes the whole rendering unshippable however good the
entries are. The rendering shipped 8 of 19 entries and does not ship as a whole,
and these two are the cheapest part of that to close: the rules exist and are
already agreed, they only had to arrive.

Closes #111

## Notes for review

- **The `Also:` line carries its own exemption.** #106 made the outcome slot
  compulsory; `output-format.md` rule 11 says the collapsed line usually has no
  outcome at all. The sentence "carries the observation alone: the three parts
  below do not apply to it" is what keeps the prompt from holding two rules that
  contradict each other.
- **Ordering is stated across the document, not within a group.** That is what
  the axis judges: a group named "What needs action" can stand at the top while
  an entry that asks something sits three groups below it.
- **Not in scope:** the outcome wording, which fails 10 of 19 entries and needs a
  different formulation rather than a rule that is missing, and the coverage rule
  behind the A1 failure, which is already in the prompt in full. Both are their
  own turn, so their effect can be read on their own axis.

facts.title: feat(cli): warn at startup when a run has no GitHub token
facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

A run that starts without a GitHub token now says so before it does any work, on stderr:

```
Warning: no GitHub token found in GITHUB_TOKEN - the run continues unauthenticated.
  GitHub allows 60 requests an hour per IP address without one, and a run
  spends roughly one per pull request, so a release can exhaust the budget
  partway through. A token raises the limit to 5000.
  Set one with: export GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token)
```

The run is not refused - a token is optional and a small release fits the anonymous budget. The message names whichever variable the run actually reads, so it stays true when `github.tokenEnvironmentVariable` was renamed, and it goes to stderr so redirecting the changelog to a file keeps it out.

`README.md` and `docs/configuration.md` now state the practical limit instead of only listing the variable.

## Why?

Closes #89.

Without a token GitHub allows 60 requests an hour per IP address, and Chartula spends roughly one per pull request. Nothing said so. The run started silently, and when the budget ran out it failed partway through with a 403 that names a commit:

```
Error: GitHub API returned 403 rate limit exceeded for commit 8061f468...
API rate limit exceeded for <ip>. (But here's the good news: Authenticated requests get a higher rate limit.)
```

The cause is one environment variable, but nothing on that path points at it - and the budget is shared with everything else reaching GitHub from that address, so the failure can arrive on a first run.

facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

`ReleaseDescription.SplitOff` no longer lifts a description out when there is
nothing under it. If striking the labelled first line would leave an empty body,
the line was not a description: the text stays the body and the description is
`null`.

```csharp
// before: "Description: All there is."  ->  ("All there is.", "")
// after:  "Description: All there is."  ->  (null, "Description: All there is.")
```

Everything else about the split is unchanged. A labelled line with one entry
under it still splits, a bolded label still counts, and text without the label is
still all body.

## Why?

The first run made after #104 produced a customer rendering of zero characters
and no `release-<tag>.md`, and reported no error:

```
technical  26320 characters
customer       0 characters
product     4327 characters
```

The run before it, on the same release and the same fact base, produced 25,457
characters of customer text.

The model was called - the run metrics report three rephrasing calls - and the
answer was then lifted out whole as the description, leaving an empty body.
From there every step behaved as designed: an empty customer body means a
release with nothing to say to that audience, so no page is written and nothing
is flagged. The rendering was gone and the run looked clean.

Ruled out on the way: the no-statements path in `ReleaseChangelogGenerator`
makes no call at all, `ChangelogFormatter` only normalises line endings and
bullet markers, `ReviewCoordinator` passes the text through while review is off,
and the customer prompt is intact. `SplitOff` is the only consumer of the
customer text that #104 added.

This does not decide why the model answered the way it did. It decides that the
answer survives either way, so the next run can be read rather than guessed at.

Closes #108

## Notes for review

- **The guard turns on the body, not on the description.** A label line with an
  empty description and entries under it keeps its existing behaviour: the line
  is consumed, the field is omitted. That case is a model leaving the line out as
  asked, which is not this one.
- **The pinning test was inverted, not deleted.**
  `A_description_on_its_own_leaves_an_empty_body` asserted the behaviour this
  fixes. It is now
  `A_line_with_nothing_under_it_is_the_body_and_not_a_description`, carrying the
  run that produced it in a comment.
- **Not in scope:** that an empty customer rendering passes through the pipeline
  without a word. It is correct for a release that genuinely has nothing for that


| `tags` | labels on the pull requests | always, for now - see #98 |

Also in this change:

- **The tag date reaches the pipeline.** `GitCliCommitReader` reads `creatordate` - the tagger date for an annotated tag, the commit date for a lightweight one - and `CommitRange` carries it. It is nullable rather than defaulted to today, because an invented date is worse than an absent field.
- **The description is written in the same call as the entries.** It is a rephrasing of facts already in front of the model, so a second call would buy nothing, and the faithfulness check covers it on the same footing as the text: the pipeline checks the description together with the body rather than beside it. The prompt asks for the line under `ReleaseDescription.Label` and the parser reads the same constant back, so a reworded prompt cannot silently lose the field.
- **A preview shows the description it would publish**, so the one field a preview could not vouch for is no longer the one that opens the page.
- **A release with no customer entries produces no page**, rather than a page with an empty body.
- **The page is written under `--no-publish`** like the other local outputs. Writing a file a person could publish is not publishing it, so there is nothing for that flag to hold back.

## Why?

The customer rendering was generated, checked for faithfulness, reviewed - and then written nowhere. It existed only as a field inside `changelog.json`, so the audience the tool exists for had no output a person could publish, and a consumer had to read the JSON and build the page themselves, which is the work the tool is supposed to have done.

Measured, not assumed: on the rendering of 2026-09-03 the evaluation harness fails the grouping axis on the missing opening, and the same document with front matter prepended by hand passes it with nothing else changed.

Closes #103

## Notes for review

- **`changelog.json` is unchanged.** The description lives on the page and not in the record, so a fixture replayed from `changelog.json` cannot reconstruct the page's opening. Carrying per-audience metadata in the JSON is a shape decision of its own and would touch the documented format; it is not needed for a publishable file and is left out here deliberately rather than overlooked.
- **The description is not presented for review.** Review returns one string, so the body is what a reviewer edits. The description still goes through the faithfulness check and is printed in the run's output.
- **Out of scope, as the issue says:** the product audience (no written template), the file serialisation of the customer rendering (many releases in one document), where the file is written to beyond the working directory, and #98.

facts.title: feat(output): write a run's artefacts without publishing a release
facts.description:
## What does this PR do?

Adds `chartula generate --no-publish`. It writes `changelog.json` and `CHANGELOG.md` and leaves the release notes untouched, and the run names what it skipped next to what it wrote:

```
Wrote:
  - changelog.json
  - CHANGELOG.md
Skipped (--no-publish):
  - Release notes for v1.0.0 in octo/repo
```

Without the flag nothing changes: `generate` writes and publishes, `preview` writes nothing.

## Why?

A run either wrote nothing or wrote everything and published. `changelog.json` is not a by-product - it is the only machine-readable record of what a run was given and what it produced - and getting it should not require announcing a release for the tag. Where no release exists yet, `GitHubReleaseNotesWriter` creates one, so today a `generate` against this repository would publish its first release as a side effect of producing a record.

That blocks two things: measuring a prompt change means rendering the same release repeatedly, and every one of those runs would rewrite the public release notes of a tag that is not being re-released; and #95 asks for a `CHANGELOG.md` explicitly without a GitHub release.

Closes #100

## How it works

- `PipelineMode` gains a third value, `GenerateWithoutPublishing`. The mode already documents itself as "how a pipeline run treats its outputs", which is exactly what differs here - so no third verb, and nothing new on `ReleaseRequest`.
- `ReleasePipeline.WriteOutputsAsync` writes the two files in both generate modes and calls `IReleaseNotesWriter` only for `Generate`. What it left out goes into the new `ReleaseOutcome.SkippedOutputs` (an `init` property defaulting to `[]`, so existing construction is unchanged).
- CLI: `CommandLineArguments.HasFlag`, plus `Program.ParseMode(command, args)` so the flag-to-mode mapping is testable, and the help text is now a `Program.Usage` string a test can hold to what the CLI accepts.

One judgement call the issue left open: `preview --no-publish` stays an ordinary preview rather than an error. Preview publishes nothing anyway, so the flag's promise holds, and the tool does not validate unknown flags elsewhere.

facts.title: fix(llm): state the shape of a customer entry instead of leaving it to the model
facts.description:
Part of #96. Customer audience only - see *What this does not do* below, and please do not let it auto-close the issue.

## What

The customer audience carried one sentence about tone and nothing about shape:

```csharp
private const string AudienceCustomer =
    "Audience: Customer. Focus on what changed for the user in plain language.";
```

It now carries the shape as well: the groups and their order, that every fact arriving has to be carried, the entry built from four parts, the openings that are not allowed, whose knowledge the reader may be assumed to have, and where a setting has to be named.

## Why these rules and not others

Each one answers a failure that was counted, not one that seemed likely. The evaluation harness scored 53 entries across three renderings by hand and then with a judge; the figures are in [`docs/targets.md`](https://github.com/goldbarth/chartula-evals/blob/main/docs/targets.md) and the rules themselves in [`docs/output-format.md`](https://github.com/goldbarth/chartula-evals/blob/main/docs/output-format.md).

| Failure | Count | Rule added |
|---|---|---|
| The closing clause restates the opening instead of stating an outcome | 19 of 53 | the strike test |
| An expression only a contributor would know | 15 of 53 | how the reader would have met it |
| The entry opens on the work that was done | 8 of 53 | the forbidden openings, named |
| An option announced with nowhere to act on it | 8 of 53 | the place, or leave the option out |
| A change carried by no entry at all | every rendering | carry every fact that arrives |
| An entry that asks something, below entries that do not | 2 of 3 | route it into the first group |
| Entries running on past their outcome | every rendering | two sentences, and stop at the outcome |

Not one of the three renderings ships whole, and four models do not differ in kind - which is the point. This was never a model choosing badly.

## Two decisions worth reviewing

**Two clauses are tests, not lists.** What counts as an outcome, and what counts as an expression the reader has already met. A list of forbidden cases is never finished, and the first case outside it gets the wrong verdict - naming the outcome slot alone had already produced *"so text completes properly"*, which is the opening negated.

**No category is named.** `categories.names` lets a user rename any category and `GroundedFactsFactory` prefixes each fact with the configured display name, so a rule saying *"a fix goes to Bug Fixes"* would break for whoever renamed `Fix`. The groups are defined by what a change is instead. For the same reason the prompt does not restate which changes appear at all: the user-visible filter in `GroundedFactsFactory` already decides that, and putting it in prose too would be the same rule in two places.

## Tests

Fourteen new tests, asserting shape rather than content - the acceptance criterion the old ones could not meet, since they would not have caught any of the three variants in the issue.

Eleven fail if the format block is removed. The other three are guards: Technical and Product stay untouched, the content rules still apply to every audience, and no category is named. Whitespace is collapsed before asserting, so a rule can be re-wrapped without breaking a test.

```
dotnet build -c Release    0 warnings, 0 errors
dotnet test  -c Release    330 passed
```

## What this does not do

- **Technical and Product are untouched.** They state tone alone, because they have no written specification. Inventing a shape for an audience nobody has specified would be the same defect as leaving it to the model, only harder to notice. Two of the issue's acceptance criteria stay open for them, including the Keep a Changelog question.
- **It does not yet prove reproducibility across runs and models.** That is the second acceptance criterion and it is a measurement, not a claim. The next step is to re-render v0.1.0 with this prompt and count against the seven figures above; `judge/count.py` in the harness does that without anyone labelling by hand.
